findings.title: Later revocation can extend the written import-validity interval
findings.diagnosis: V6 section 2 uses an unconditional assignment of valid_until to the revoking event time. It does not state first-revocation-wins or minimum-with-existing-end. Section 4 makes membership in this interval the import-time authority predicate. With more than one applicable invalidation, a literal overwrite widens the interval and can fail to create UNAUTHORIZED_DISPATCH for an already-revoked delayed launch. Retained v3 active-lease and v6 replay prose prohibit revival, so this is an internal specification conflict, not proof that every conforming interpretation authorizes the launch. The issue was inherited from v5 and is newly identified here.

evidence.observation: Revocation sets valid_until to the revoking event time; authorization is valid_from <= t < valid_until. No minimum or first-event update rule is stated.
Complete reconciliation list delegates launch-time authority to the interval in section 2.
Retained lease validity requires no later rewind and time below the original maximum. Revoked reservation must start nothing. These oppose interval revival.
V5 already uses lease-end validity and revocation assignment. This is newly noticed inherited ambiguity, not a new v6 regression.

Literal SET accepts launch 50 after revocation 40 when a later revocation sets end 60. Minimum-end negative control rejects. The decisive sequence uses two nonterminal legal rewinds; the original terminal illustration was self-challenged and preserved.

reproduction_or_attack: At time 10, authentic approved generation G1 has original end 100. Reserve dispatch I; charge once.
At 40, human-approved rewind to ROUTE_SELECTION revokes G1. Its effective end must now remain at most 40.
At 50, a delayed trusted scheduler accidentally launches I without a fresh successful hook. The launch is visible in the declared ledger namespace. Such omission must be detected at import under T.
At 60, human approves a further rewind to PLANNING, legal from Route selection. An importer that applies the section 2 assignment to each affected record overwrites I.valid_until with 60.
Subsequent legitimate plan/route/authorization approvals and a fresh review can reach a nonterminal import checkpoint. Scan the entire namespace as required.
The literal interval 10 <= 50 < 60 accepts I. The earliest-end interval 10 <= 50 < 40 refuses and creates UNAUTHORIZED_DISPATCH BLOCK. No human approved the launch at 50.
Independent second boundary: original expiry 20, delayed launch 30, later policy-change event 40. Replacing expiry by 40 also accepts what the original wall-time bound rejects.
findings.expected: Effective end is the earliest original expiry and all applicable revocation times for that authority generation. It never increases. Delayed launches after the first end create UNAUTHORIZED_DISPATCH BLOCK at import, even after subsequent valid human reauthorization.
findings.actual: Single-event endpoints are corrected. Multiple-event composition is not given a monotone reducer. A literal section 2/4 implementation accepts the counterexample; an implementation enforcing retained no-revival semantics rejects it. The operative rules need one consistent answer.
findings.closure_criterion: State valid_until = min(original_expiry, all applicable revocation times), or an equivalent first-revocation terminal rule. Preserve generation identity. Model two revocations in chronological/reverse ingestion order, expiry then later revocation, later renewal, equality ties and the valid-before-earliest-end control. Assign the resulting tests to internal/host import at Gate C (and lease-generation integration at Gate D). No future runtime execution is required to close the Gate A design finding.

fix.action: Amend v6 section 2 so every revocation can only shorten an authority generation: effective_valid_until = min(original_valid_until, prior_effective_valid_until, event_time). An expired/revoked generation never becomes active on later rewind, terminal record, policy event or renewal; new authority requires a separately approved generation. Add TestLaterRevocationCannotExtendValidity and TestExpiryNotExtendedByLaterRevocation to the internal/host import proof row.
fix.why: This makes the explicit reconciliation algorithm agree with the retained original-expiry and no-later-rewind requirements. It detects ordinary delayed launch/host drift under T without adding a tamper-resistant launcher.

verification.method: G1 issued at 10/end100, rewind40, visible delayed launch50, second nonterminal rewind60, later authentic G2 authorization; reconcile G1 ledger at a nonterminal checkpoint.
verification.expected: G1 end stays40; I is UNAUTHORIZED_DISPATCH BLOCK; G2 cannot retroactively authorize I.

verification.method: Expiry20, launch30, later revocation40; test reverse ingestion order as well.
verification.expected: End stays20 in every order; launch30 refused.

verification.method: Launch just before earliest end, exactly at it and after it; replay final reserved slot before any invalidation.
verification.expected: Before-earliest-end positive control accepted; equality/after refused; valid final-slot replay remains available once without new charge.

fix.tradeoffs: Small design correction and a small future reducer/test addition. It is conservative at timestamp ties. It must use the original authority generation rather than a later renewal. No new approval field, changed threat model or broader permission is needed. Literal-model success does not validate future production code.
fix.alternative: Make each authority generation a terminal state machine after its first effective revocation, with immutable original expiry and explicit generation IDs. This also prevents revival, but a minimum projection over existing event times is smaller.
